answers.label: Q1(a)
answers.finalAnswer: Corona-phobia: a fear of the deadly, invisible disease that has gripped the whole world alike.
answers.solution: COVID-19 has created 'corona-phobia' in our minds: a fear of catching the deadly disease and even of mankind being wiped out like the dinosaurs. This fear has gripped the whole world, whatever a person's caste, colour or religion.

answers.label: Q1(b)
answers.finalAnswer: We are caught in a dilemma: stay indoors to be safe and starve, or go out to earn a living at the risk of our lives.
answers.solution: Mankind is caught between the devil and the deep blue sea. To protect ourselves from the pandemic we must stay indoors, but then we cannot earn and may starve. To earn a living we must go out, even at the risk of our lives.

answers.label: Q1(c)
answers.finalAnswer: Not to give in to fear, to prepare for the worst, to do our duty no matter what, and to face challenges bravely but not foolishly.
answers.solution: Soldiers prepare for the worst and never surrender to fear. They do not sit indoors thinking only of their safety; they go out and do their duty no matter what. From them we must learn to psych ourselves up and face the pandemic fearlessly, but not foolishly.

answers.label: Q1(d)
answers.finalAnswer: Face it fearlessly but not foolishly, keep working, improve our immunity and learn to live with it.
answers.solution: We can deal with the pandemic by facing it fearlessly but not foolishly, going out to work with proper care, improving our immunity and learning how to live with the disease. Then the enemy's days will be numbered.

answers.label: Q1(e)
answers.finalAnswer: (i) go the way of the dinosaurs; (ii) take the bull by the horns; (iii) caught between the devil and the deep blue sea
answers.solution:
(i) to become extinct: **go the way of the dinosaurs**
(ii) to face a difficulty bravely: **take the bull by the horns**
(iii) be in a dilemma: **(be) caught between the devil and the deep blue sea**

answers.label: Q1(f)
answers.finalAnswer: No. It respects no man-made barriers such as caste, colour, ethnicity or religion, and attacks everyone alike.
answers.solution: No, the pandemic is not partial. It has no respect for man-made barriers such as caste, colour, ethnicity or religion. It can attack anyone, and the whole world is united by the same fear of it.

answers.label: Q1(g)
answers.finalAnswer: Like soldiers, we should face the pandemic with courage and care, keep working, build our immunity and learn to live with it; all is not lost.
answers.solution: The passage tells us not to let fear rule us. Like soldiers, we should face the pandemic bravely but sensibly, keep working because work is life, improve our immunity and learn to live with the disease. All is not lost.

answers.label: Q.2(a)
answers.finalAnswer: The Fearless Little Rabbit
answers.solution: A suitable title: **"The Fearless Little Rabbit"**, because the poem is about a young rabbit who refuses to live in fear.

answers.label: Q.2(b)
answers.finalAnswer: Repetition
answers.solution:
**Repetition**: the line "My parents tell me not to go out" is repeated at the start of the stanzas. (Personification is also used: a rabbit speaks and thinks like a person.)

(The first line is misprinted "no to go out" for "not to go out".)

answers.label: Q.2(c)
answers.finalAnswer: Stay at home, not go out, and obey them so that he is safe from animals, birds, illness and injury and is successful in future.
answers.solution: The parents want the rabbit to stay at home and not go out, because he could be killed by a tiger, carried off by an eagle, or fall ill or get hurt. They want him to obey them so that he is safe and successful in future.

answers.label: Q.2(d)
answers.finalAnswer: He is fearless and lives in the present: he accepts nature and destiny, loves playing with friends and does not want to live in fear.
answers.solution: The rabbit is fearless and lives for the present. He accepts that he is part of nature's food chain and that destiny has its own plans, so he does not fear tigers, eagles, illness or injury. He loves playing with his friends and says "now is important to me"; he does not want to live in fear.

answers.label: Q.2(e)
answers.finalAnswer: The parents are angry that he disobeys them, but they scold him out of love and worry for his safety.
answers.solution: The parents are angry because the rabbit keeps going out against their wishes, but their anger comes from love: they scold him because they care about him and fear for his safety.

answers.label: Q.2(f)
answers.finalAnswer: Do not let fear stop you from living and enjoying the present.
answers.solution: The moral of the poem is that we should not let fear stop us from living. Life is lived in the present, and a life spent in fear is not truly lived, even though parents' warnings come from love.

answers.label: Q.3
answers.solution:
**Title: Education Turns Uniqueness into Talent**

Almost every great thinker has defined education, and all agree that it teaches us valuable lessons for life. It widens our outlook and shows us our abilities as individuals and our role as citizens. Its chief aim is to bring out the best in each person. Since every human being is unique, schooling must discover this uniqueness and help it grow into a talent; if it is neglected, it may become a vice. Thus good education grooms uniqueness into talent.

(77 words)

answers.label: Q.4
answers.solution:
(Two topics chosen: (a) and (b).)

**(a) Genius is an Infinite Capacity for Taking Pains**

Many people believe that geniuses are simply born brilliant. Thomas Carlyle disagreed. He said that genius is an infinite capacity for taking pains, which means that greatness comes from endless hard work.

History proves him right. Thomas Edison failed thousands of times before his electric bulb worked, and he called genius "one per cent inspiration and ninety-nine per cent perspiration". Sachin Tendulkar practised for hours every day, even after he became a star. Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam rose from a poor family in Rameswaram through patient study and sincere effort.

Natural talent is like a seed. Without the water of hard work, it never grows into a tree. An ordinary student who works steadily, learns from mistakes and never gives up can achieve extraordinary things.

So we should not wait for luck. We should work patiently and take pains, for that is the real secret of genius.

**(b) Technology is Making Us Unsocial**

Technology has made our lives faster and easier. With one tap we can talk to a cousin abroad or order food. Yet many people feel that it is making us unsocial.

Look at any family at the dinner table today. Often each member is busy with a phone instead of talking to the others. Children prefer video games to playing outdoors with friends. Many people have hundreds of 'friends' online but nobody to share a real problem with. Even at weddings and festivals, people are busier taking photographs than meeting relatives.

However, technology itself is not the villain. It helped families stay in touch during the lockdown, and it lets us find old friends. The problem is how we use it.

We must set limits: no phones at meals, and time every day for outdoor games and real conversation. Technology should bring us together, not keep us apart.

answers.label: Q.5
answers.solution:
**A Lesson on the Wrong Train**

Last month I had to go to Mumbai by train to attend an interview. I left home in good time, but on the way my taxi got stuck in a huge traffic jam. By the time I reached the railway station, I was very late.

A train was just leaving from platform two. Without checking the board, I ran and jumped into it. I sat down and sighed with relief. When the ticket checker came, I put my hand in my pocket. My wallet was gone! Worse, he told me that the train was going to Pune, not Mumbai.

I had realised my mistakes too late. I got down at the next station, called my father and explained everything to the interview office. They kindly gave me another date.

Now I always leave home early and check the train twice before boarding.

answers.label: Q.6
answers.solution:
25, Rajpur Road
Dehradun
15 February 2020

Dear Meera,

I hope you are enjoying your stay with your grandparents in Kerala. I am writing to tell you all about our school's Annual Day, which was held last Saturday.

The function began with the lighting of the lamp by our chief guest, the District Collector. Then came a colourful programme of songs, dances and a play. I was the anchor for the whole evening. I was nervous at first, but soon I began to enjoy it. Our class also performed a folk dance from Punjab, which won loud applause.

We all missed you a lot. You would have sung the welcome song so beautifully, and our dance team badly needed you. Everyone kept asking, "Where is Meera?"

I have kept some photographs to show you. Come back soon.

Your loving friend,
Ananya

answers.label: Q.7
answers.solution:
**Social Media Causes More Harm than Good (For)**

Social media was created to bring people closer, but today it causes more harm than good.

First, it wastes a great deal of time. Students spend hours scrolling through videos and posts when they should be studying, sleeping or playing outdoors. Second, it spreads fake news very quickly, and rumours shared on it have even led to violence. Third, it harms our minds. Young people compare their lives with the perfect pictures of others and feel sad and lonely, and cyberbullying has left many children frightened. Finally, sharing personal details online puts our privacy and safety at risk.

It is true that social media helps us stay in touch and learn new things, but these benefits are small compared to the damage it does. Therefore, I firmly believe that social media causes more harm than good.

answers.finalAnswer: Claustrophobia; Encyclopaedia; Pandemic; Swarm; Utopia
answers.solution:
(a) Fear of confined places: **claustrophobia**
(b) A book that contains information on various subjects: **encyclopaedia**
(c) A disease which spreads over a wide geographical area in a large proportion of the population: **pandemic**
(d) A large group of insects moving in a mass: **swarm**
(e) An imaginary ideal society free of poverty and suffering: **utopia**

answers.label: Q.9
answers.finalAnswer: the; the; Ø; an; Ø; a; the; a; a; The; Ø; the; the; The; Ø; the; Ø; Ø; a; a
answers.solution:
(a) Moving to (i) **the** United States was (ii) **the** most exciting thing I have ever done. I moved last year to (iii) **Ø** New York. New York is (iv) **an** exciting city, full of (v) **Ø** adventure. In fact, I saw (vi) **a** famous actor on (vii) **the** street yesterday!

(b) Today I have (viii) **a** job interview at (ix) **a** financial company. (x) **The** company has (xi) **Ø** offices all over (xii) **the** world. I'm not sure that I have (xiii) **the** skills to get hired. I hope so. (xiv) **The** company's office is on (xv) **Ø** Main Street. That's (xvi) **the** same street my friend works on.

(c) If I get hired, I could meet him after (xvii) **Ø** work for drinks. That would be great. He's from (xviii) **Ø** Scotland. He works 8 hours (xix) **a** day, 5 days (xx) **a** week.

Rules used: 'the' before country names that are plural or contain 'States', before superlatives, before 'world', before something already mentioned (the company) and before 'same'; no article before names of cities, countries like Scotland, streets, or 'work' used generally; 'a'/'an' for one of many (a job interview, an exciting city) and to mean 'per' (a day, a week).

answers.label: Q.11
answers.finalAnswer: (i) banking on; (iii) bear out; (ii) call upon; (i) break up; (iv) taken aback; (ii) asking for
answers.solution:
(a) She is **banking on** the bank loan for her higher studies. (depending on)
(b) Modern researches **bear out** that yoga cures diseases. (confirm)
(c) Many people **call upon** God for help rather than to thank him. (appeal to)
(d) The police were called in to **break up** the rioters. (scatter)
(e) I was **taken aback** when I topped the merit list. (surprised)
(f) He is **asking for** trouble if he quarrels with the house owner. (inviting)

Part (c) is defective as printed: the blank is followed by "to God", which fits none of the options, and options (ii) "call upon" and (iv) "call on" mean the same thing (appeal to). "Call upon" is taken as the intended answer.

answers.label: Q.14
answers.finalAnswer: (iv) with; (ii) to; (iv) no preposition needed; (ii) with; (ii) of; (ii) on; (iii) into, by
answers.solution:
(a) Tagore was endowed **with** rare talents.
(b) You are not amenable **to** reason.
(c) He emphasised his point. (**no preposition**: 'emphasise' takes a direct object; 'emphasis on' is the noun form)
(d) I beg to differ **with** you on this subject.
(e) The poor old man was blind **of** one eye. (the traditional usage in grammar books; modern English also says 'blind in one eye')
(f) My friend insisted **on** my staying with her a little longer.
(g) Entry **into** this auditorium is **by** ticket.
